problems: PROMPT/SCENARIO MISMATCH (metadata defect, not a page defect): the task prompt describes an entirely DIFFERENT case than what is on disk. Prompt claims an 'E-commerce running-shoe store' instant-search counter wired role=alert (assertive 'too chatty'), selector p#liveCount[role="alert"], cited against the Understanding 'too chatty' passage. The ACTUAL files are a 'Helmsley Workspace' notification-preferences page with a save-confirmation banner wired aria-live="off", selector span#savedMsg[aria-live="off"], cited against F103. The .md (lines 100-115) explicitly documents that the old role=alert scenario was REJECTED by a prior adversarial reviewer as advisory/non-normative and rewritten to the aria-live="off" F103 scenario. So the prompt is stale; I reviewed the file that actually exists.

The selector in the prompt (p#liveCount[role="alert"]) does not exist on the page; the real defect element is span#savedMsg[aria-live="off"] (HTML line 93). The prompt's claimed mechanism (assertive per-keystroke clobbering) and claimed citation (Understanding 'too chatty') do not apply to this page at all.

Minor/disclosed: the cited Understanding file wcag-understanding/status-messages.html has <h1> 'Status Messages' with draft numbering 3.2.6 (WCAG 2.1 draft id for 4.1.3); the .md discloses this honestly and relies on F103 as the primary normative citation, so it is not a material defect.

Citation nuance (not a defect, but worth noting): SCR14's own example markup uses the IDENTICAL configuration as the test page (aria-live="assertive" + aria-atomic="true" + setInterval). The quoted SCR14 *objective* sentence does not by itself convey why this page FAILS; the actual basis for failure is SCR14's Test Procedure — 'Load the web page and verify that no non-emergency alerts are displayed' and 'Verify there is a mechanism to activate and deactivate the non-emergency interruptions' — both of which the page violates (alerts fire by default; no toggle exists). A reviewer relying only on the quoted objective could mistakenly read SCR14 as endorsing the page's assertive markup.

The page conflates two distinct remedies in its narrative: the .md/HTML comments argue the fix is 'polite' politeness, while the cited SCR14 technique's remedy is a toggle (keep assertive but make it opt-out). Both are valid 4.1.3 cures, but the doc could be clearer that the defect is 'non-essential, interrupting status with neither reduced politeness nor an opt-out mechanism.'

Minor: the documented mechanism leans on an 'ongoing long narration race' premise (the polite update queuing behind #terms speech), which is AT/timing-dependent and not guaranteed on every screen reader. The SC failure does not actually require the race — wiring a time-critical, action-blocking session-expiry countdown as aria-live=polite is itself the defect (polite is by design deferrable/suppressible per Understanding doc line 42). The doc's framing is fine and strengthens the verdict, but the race is presented as more deterministic than it is.

PROMPT/METADATA MISMATCH (critical): The prompt describes a DIFFERENT page than what is on disk. Prompt claims an LMS essay autosave indicator wired role=alert (over-assertive, 'too chatty'), selector span#autosave[role="alert"], with a citation about applications being 'too chatty'. The actual case-04.html is a MercyHealth refill form whose role=status region #refillStatus is muted to aria-live="off" by an on-by-default 'Focus mode' toggle (F103, the OPPOSITE direction: under-announced, not over-assertive). The prompt's selector span#autosave does not exist on the page (no role=alert anywhere; the element is p#refillStatus[role=status]). The prompt's claimed mechanism and citation do not apply to this file.

I evaluated the ACTUAL on-disk page. It is a genuine, internally-coherent SC 4.1.3 FAILED case (F103): applyFocusMode(true) at line 114 sets aria-live="off" (line 112) at load; the submit handler (lines 121-131) injects a consequential 'Refill request FAILED...' status message into the muted region, so AT announces nothing. Confirmed by runtime probe (region stays aria-live=off through submit in the default state; flips to polite only after manual toggle) and the Chromium AX tree (role:status, aria-live:off).

The .md doc's two citations are verbatim and on-point (F103 objective sentence in wcag-techniques/failures/F103.html; Understanding-Intent sentence in wcag-understanding/status-messages.html) — but they belong to the on-disk F103 page, NOT to the prompt's assertive-chatty scenario. The prompt's quoted citation ('too chatty... user testing should be carried out') is not what the page is about.

Outcome-label nuance (does NOT change the verdict): real-world AT handling of aria-atomic on live regions is inconsistent (some screen readers re-read the whole region regardless). The page's 'failed' is defensible because the author explicitly defeated the spec-default atomic behavior and the spec-conformant result is a truncated 'two' announcement; the .md correctly notes this is the failing inverse of the ARIA22-passing pattern.

Minor caveat (not a defect): real-world AT behavior for aria-atomic=false on role=status is environment-dependent — ARIA22 line 22 itself notes role=status 'is currently not treated as atomic by default in some environments', and some SR/browser pairs may still re-read the whole region. The page's claimed 'bare 85' announcement is the spec-correct and most common outcome, so the 'failed' verdict holds, but exact announced phrasing varies by screen reader.

Cosmetic: line 41's HTML comment writes aria-atomic="FALSE" (uppercase) as persona narrative; the actual element under test (line 46) uses lowercase aria-atomic="false". ARIA boolean tokens are case-insensitive anyway and the live probe resolved it to false, so no functional impact — noting only that source comment vs. live attribute differ in casing.

Minor doc imprecision (not a defect to the verdict): the .md 'Exact accessibility mechanism' says role=status is 'spec-atomic by default,' which overstates — the spec/ARIA22 note is precisely that atomicity is NOT reliably honored across environments. The cited quotes are accurate; only the prose summary is loose. The failed verdict holds regardless, because the failure is partial-region update (only the numeral chunk is coded as the updated content), which is non-equivalent to the visible whole even under an atomic AT policy.

Conditional-on-environment caveat (not a defect, but noting for honesty): the failure assumes a non-atomic AT/browser environment. ARIA22 (line 22 of the cited file) states role=status is 'currently not treated as atomic by default in SOME environments' — modern Chromium/NVDA/JAWS combos may honor the atomic default and announce the full '267 characters remaining'. The doc and ARIA22 both acknowledge this unreliability, so authoring it as a failure (reliance on an unreliable default) is defensible and ACT-consistent — but the bare-'267' outcome is not universal across all AT.

The flattened AX-tree walk surfaced the 'Post' button text adjacent to the status region; a direct DOM probe confirmed buttonInside=false (the button is a sibling of p#meter, NOT inside the live region), so there is no real over-announcement bug. Recorded only to document that the apparent containment was a tree-walk artifact, not a page defect.

Minor normative nuance (not a defect): SC 4.1.3's strict normative text concerns whether status messages are *programmatically determinable* via role/properties so they're presented without focus — which this region technically satisfies (valid role=status before update, valid aria-live/atomic, announced atomically). The actual failure is contextual-sufficiency of the announced text ('three' with no noun). The corpus correctly anchors this to ARIA22 test-procedure step 3 (visual-equivalent context such as the cart image+alt must reside INSIDE the container — it does not) and the Understanding's 'only hear three' example, so 'failed' is defensible under an ACT/technique reading, but a purist could file it as a sufficiency/quality issue rather than a hard normative 4.1.3 violation.
The in-page '.note' div narrates 'why automated tools pass' inside the rendered DOM; harmless for the element under test (#cartCount) but means the page literally describes its own bug.

The claimed failure is about SUFFICIENCY of the announced content (percentage without ticker), which WCAG Understanding addresses in advisory 'authors may wish to' language ('Non-displayed text specific to AT users') rather than hard normative SC text. 'failed' is defensible and well-supported by the cited Understanding sections, but the case sits near the normative/advisory line — correctly flagged as requiring human judgment.
